starters.name: Water
starters.description: Fresh water for drinking, boiling, and mixing.

starters.name: Fruits
starters.description: Tree and vine fruits picked ripe from the wild or grove.

starters.name: Berries
starters.description: Small sweet or tart berries gathered in clusters.

starters.name: Roots
starters.description: Edible roots and rhizomes dug from the soil.

starters.name: Tubers
starters.description: Starchy tubers — dense energy stored underground.

starters.name: Nuts
starters.description: Hard-shelled nuts and kernels rich in fat and protein.

starters.name: Shellfish
starters.description: Mollusks and crustaceans harvested from shore or shallows.

starters.name: Mushrooms
starters.description: Wild fungi foraged from forest floor and decaying wood.

starters.name: Seeds
starters.description: Dried seeds and grains — compact stores of starch and oil.

starters.name: Grasses
starters.description: Edible grasses and cereal stalks — fibrous greens and grains.

starters.name: Shoots
starters.description: Tender young shoots and sprouts — soft, fast-growing greens.

recipes.description: You plucked a single berry from the wild cluster.
recipes.tip: Mixed berry patches ripen unevenly — separate them one at a time to sort each fruit.

strawberry.name: Strawberry
strawberry.description: Sweet, fragrant red berries with soft flesh.
strawberry.blurb: Medieval Europeans believed strawberries could lift melancholy, and the name may come from the practice of mulching plants with straw.

raspberry.name: Raspberry
raspberry.description: Tart, delicate red drupelets that pull away easily from the core.
raspberry.blurb: Raspberries have been gathered across Europe since prehistoric times; the hollow core is left on the plant when you pick one.

blueberry.name: Blueberry
blueberry.description: Small round blue berries with a light bloom and balanced sweetness.
blueberry.blurb: Blueberries are one of the few truly blue foods in nature — the waxy "bloom" on the skin helps the fruit shed rainwater.

blackberry.name: Blackberry
blackberry.description: Plump dark aggregate berries with a deep, jammy flavor.
blackberry.blurb: Romans noted blackberries growing along roadsides, and English hedgerows were often planted with brambles to mark field boundaries.

recipes.description: You sorted a single ripe fruit from the wild harvest.
recipes.tip: Mixed fruit baskets hide surprises — separate them one at a time to learn what you have.

apple.name: Apple
apple.description: Crisp, sweet-tart flesh beneath thin skin.
apple.blurb: Apples spread along Silk Road trade routes and became one of the world's most cultivated tree fruits — thousands of varieties exist, but only a handful dominate grocery shelves.

banana.name: Banana
banana.description: Soft, starchy-sweet flesh in a peelable yellow jacket.
banana.blurb: Wild bananas are full of hard seeds; the smooth Cavendish banana we eat today is a sterile clone propagated by cuttings for nearly two centuries.

orange.name: Orange
orange.description: Juicy citrus segments with bright, sunny acidity.
orange.blurb: Oranges reached Europe from Southeast Asia via Arab traders; Portuguese sailors later planted them along trade winds, giving us the name for the color orange itself.

grape.name: Grape
grape.description: Plump clusters of sweet or tart juice-filled berries.
grape.blurb: Humans have cultivated grapes for wine, raisins, and fresh eating for at least 8,000 years — one of the oldest domesticated fruit crops.

pear.name: Pear
pear.description: Buttery, fragrant flesh that softens as it ripens.
pear.blurb: Pears were prized in medieval orchards for keeping well through winter — a rare fresh sweetness when snow covered the ground.

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.description: Refreshing, watery crimson flesh inside a thick rind.
watermelon.blurb: Ancient Egyptian tomb paintings depict watermelons, and seeds were found in King Tut's tomb — a prized desert refreshment long before ice existed.

mango.name: Mango
mango.description: Velvety golden flesh with honeyed tropical sweetness.
mango.blurb: India celebrates mango season with festivals and poetry; the fruit is so beloved there that a basket of mangoes is still considered a generous gift.

pineapple.name: Pineapple
pineapple.description: Fibrous, explosively sweet flesh beneath spiny armor.
pineapple.blurb: European colonists called pineapple the "king of fruits" and rented them as centerpiece displays at banquets — a symbol of wealth before refrigeration made them common.

lemon.name: Lemon
lemon.description: Sharp, aromatic juice and zest with clean acidity.
lemon.blurb: British sailors earned the nickname "limeys" for citrus rations that prevented scurvy — lemons and limes quietly changed naval history.

peach.name: Peach
peach.description: Fuzzy skin giving way to soft, fragrant, juicy flesh.
peach.blurb: Peaches originated in China, where they symbolized immortality and good fortune; silk traders carried them west along routes that shaped the ancient world.

recipes.description: You drew off a distinct kind of water from the wild source.
recipes.tip: Water looks uniform until you separate it — spring, mineral, rain, and sea each behave differently in the pot.

spring_water.name: Spring Water
spring_water.description: Naturally filtered water rising cool from underground.
spring_water.blurb: Springs were sacred sites in many cultures — clean, mineral-rich water bubbling up without a river in sight.

mineral_water.name: Mineral Water
mineral_water.description: Water carrying dissolved salts and trace minerals.
mineral_water.blurb: European spa towns built fortunes on mineral springs; the dissolved limestone and salts were thought to cure ailments.

rainwater.name: Rainwater
rainwater.description: Soft, slightly acidic water collected from the sky.
rainwater.blurb: Before wells and pipes, cisterns caught rainwater for brewing and baking — bakers prized its softness for tender crumb.

seawater.name: Seawater
seawater.description: Salty ocean water — briny and dense.
seawater.blurb: Roman fish sauce factories boiled seawater into garum; today chefs still use a pinch of sea water to season shellfish.

recipes.description: You unearthed a single edible root from the tangle below.
recipes.tip: Root patches hide many species — separate them carefully one at a time.

carrot.name: Carrot
carrot.blurb: Carrots were purple and yellow long before Dutch growers popularized the orange varieties we know today.

ginger.name: Ginger
ginger.description: Knobby rhizome with sharp, warming heat.
ginger.blurb: Ginger traveled from Southeast Asia along trade routes and became essential in medicines, candies, and curries worldwide.

beet.name: Beet
beet.description: Earthy, jewel-toned root with dense sweetness.
beet.blurb: Beet sugar once rivaled cane sugar in Europe; the same root that sweetens also stains borscht a vivid crimson.

radish.name: Radish
radish.description: Crisp, peppery root that bites back.
radish.blurb: Ancient Egyptians fed radishes to workers building the pyramids — cheap, fast-growing fuel for massive labor crews.

turnip.name: Turnip
turnip.description: Sturdy pale root with mild cabbage notes.
turnip.blurb: Turnips kept European villages fed through winter centuries before potatoes arrived from the Americas.

recipes.description: You dug up one starchy tuber from the mound.
recipes.tip: Tuber piles look alike underground — separate them to sort each variety.

potato.name: Potato
potato.description: Neutral, fluffy starch that loves heat and fat.
potato.blurb: Potatoes from the Andes transformed European agriculture — a single plant that could feed whole villages through winter.

sweet_potato.name: Sweet Potato
sweet_potato.description: Orange flesh with caramel sweetness when roasted.
sweet_potato.blurb: Despite the name, sweet potatoes are only distantly related to potatoes — Polynesian voyagers carried them across the Pacific.

yam.name: Yam
yam.description: Large, starchy tuber with dry, dense flesh.
yam.blurb: In West Africa yams are celebration food — annual festivals mark the harvest of tubers that can grow larger than a person's arm.

taro.name: Taro
taro.description: Starchy corm with nutty flavor when properly cooked.
taro.blurb: Taro sustained Pacific island cultures for millennia; poi made from taro root remains central to Hawaiian tradition.

cassava.name: Cassava
cassava.description: Tropical root that must be processed to remove bitterness.
cassava.blurb: Also called manioc or yuca, cassava feeds hundreds of millions — tapioca pearls and farinha both begin with this hardy root.

recipes.description: You cracked out a single nut from the wild harvest.
recipes.tip: Mixed nuts rattle together — separate them one shell at a time.

almond.name: Almond
almond.description: Mild, milky kernel beneath a papery skin.
almond.blurb: Almond orchards need honeybee pollination — entire truckloads of hives travel California valleys each spring.

walnut.name: Walnut
walnut.description: Rich, tannic nut with a lobed brain-like shape.
walnut.blurb: Walnut trees release juglone into the soil, discouraging rivals — gardeners still plant them downwind of vegetable beds.

pecan.name: Pecan
pecan.description: Buttery Southern nut with sweet maple notes.
pecan.blurb: Pecan pie became an American icon, but the trees are native only to the Mississippi valley and northern Mexico.

hazelnut.name: Hazelnut
hazelnut.description: Toasty round nut prized in confections.
hazelnut.blurb: Turkey grows most of the world's hazelnuts; Nutella alone consumes a significant share of the global crop.

pistachio.name: Pistachio
pistachio.description: Green kernel with a split shell and savory richness.
pistachio.blurb: Pistachios open on the tree when ripe — harvesters shake the branches and catch nuts that have naturally "smiled" open.

recipes.description: You picked out one fungus from the foraged cluster.
recipes.tip: Never rush a mushroom basket — separate and identify each find one at a time.

button_mushroom.name: Button Mushroom
button_mushroom.description: Pale, mild cultivated mushroom with firm cap.
button_mushroom.blurb: Agaricus bisporus appears as white buttons, brown cremini, and giant portobellos — all the same species at different ages.

shiitake.name: Shiitake
shiitake.description: Umami-rich cap with a smoky, savory aroma.
shiitake.blurb: Shiitake have been cultivated on oak logs in Japan for over a thousand years — "shii" refers to the pasania oak they prefer.

oyster_mushroom.name: Oyster Mushroom
oyster_mushroom.description: Delicate fan-shaped mushroom with subtle seafood notes.
oyster_mushroom.blurb: Oyster mushrooms grow in shelf-like clusters on dead trees and are now farmed on straw — one of the easiest fungi to cultivate.

portobello.name: Portobello
portobello.description: Large mature cap with meaty texture for grilling.
portobello.blurb: Marketing renamed overgrown brown cremini "portobello" in the 1980s — a rebranding trick that launched the stuffed mushroom craze.

chanterelle.name: Chanterelle
chanterelle.description: Golden trumpet mushroom with fruity, peppery perfume.
chanterelle.blurb: Chanterelles resist domestication — foragers still hunt them in mossy forests, and chefs pay premium prices for wild baskets.

recipes.description: You threshed out a single grain from the wild grasses.
recipes.tip: A handful of grasses holds many cereals — separate them stalk by stalk.

wheat.name: Wheat
wheat.description: Golden grain that forms the backbone of bread.
wheat.blurb: Wheat agriculture began in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000 years ago and reshaped human settlement into cities.

barley.name: Barley
barley.description: Chewy grain with malty depth — beer's oldest base.
barley.blurb: Ancient Sumerian brewers fermented barley bread into beer; monks and farmers alike relied on barley soups through harsh winters.

oats.name: Oats
oats.description: Mild, creamy grain prized for porridge.
oats.blurb: Oats were once considered weed grain in wheat fields until Scottish highlanders turned them into a staple porridge culture.

rice.name: Rice
rice.description: Starchy kernel that feeds billions across humid climates.
rice.blurb: Terraced rice paddies sculpt Asian landscapes — flooded fields suppress weeds while the grain sustains more than half the world.

rye.name: Rye
rye.description: Hardy dark grain with tangy, robust flavor.
rye.blurb: Rye thrives where wheat struggles — Nordic rye breads and Russian black bread survived winters that killed other crops.

recipes.description: You clipped a single tender shoot from the bundle.
recipes.tip: Young shoots look alike at a glance — separate them gently one by one.

asparagus.name: Asparagus
asparagus.description: Spears with grassy sweetness and delicate snap.
asparagus.blurb: Asparagus beds take three years to mature but can produce for decades — Roman emperors had special fleets fetch fresh spears.

bamboo_shoot.name: Bamboo Shoot
bamboo_shoot.description: Crisp, mild shoot harvested before the cane hardens.
bamboo_shoot.blurb: Bamboo grows so fast you can almost hear it — shoots must be boiled to remove bitterness before stir-frying.

pea_shoot.name: Pea Shoot
pea_shoot.description: Curly tendrils with fresh pea flavor.
pea_shoot.blurb: Chefs prize pea shoots in spring — the same plant gives peas later, but the tips are sweetest while still climbing.

alfalfa_sprout.name: Alfalfa Sprout
alfalfa_sprout.description: Mild, crunchy sprout packed with green flavor.
alfalfa_sprout.blurb: Sprouted seeds multiply vitamins and enzymes — alfalfa sprouts became a health-food icon on 1970s sandwiches.

watercress.name: Watercress
watercress.description: Peppery aquatic green with bright bite.
watercress.blurb: Watercress grows in clean running water — Victorian London sold it street-side as a cheap, vitamin-rich working-class green.

recipes.description: You sorted a single seed type from the dried harvest.
recipes.tip: Seed sacks hold mixtures — separate them to learn what will sprout or roast.

sunflower_seed.name: Sunflower Seed
sunflower_seed.description: Nutty kernel rich in oil — snack or press.
sunflower_seed.blurb: Indigenous North Americans bred sunflowers for oil and food long before European contact — seeds still follow the sun in the field.

pumpkin_seed.name: Pumpkin Seed
pumpkin_seed.description: Flat green pepita with toasty flavor.
pumpkin_seed.blurb: Mexican pepitas flavor moles and snacks; carving pumpkins at Halloween leaves tons of seeds worth roasting with salt.

sesame.name: Sesame
sesame.description: Tiny oilseed that becomes tahini and crunch.
sesame.blurb: "Open sesame" reflects the seed pods that burst when ripe — sesame may be the oldest oilseed crop humans ever cultivated.

flax.name: Flax
flax.description: Glossy brown seed yielding oil and fiber.
flax.blurb: Linen fabric comes from flax stalks while the seeds give linseed oil — the same plant dressed ancient Egypt and fed livestock.

chia.name: Chia
chia.description: Microseed that swells into a gel when soaked.
chia.blurb: Aztec runners carried chia for endurance; today the same mucilaginous gel thickens puddings and health drinks.

recipes.description: You pulled one shellfish from the tidepool catch.
recipes.tip: Mixed shore harvests need sorting — separate each creature carefully.

shrimp.name: Shrimp
shrimp.description: Sweet, quick-cooking crustacean with firm snap.
shrimp.blurb: Shrimp fisheries span every temperate coast — they turn pink in seconds on heat, a telltale sign their pigments are released.

oyster.name: Oyster
oyster.description: Briny bivalve eaten raw or gently cooked.
oyster.blurb: Oysters filter gallons of water daily — reef restoration projects now plant them to clean polluted harbors.

clam.name: Clam
clam.description: Burrowing bivalve with sweet, tender meat.
clam.blurb: New England clam chowder and Italian vongole pasta both begin with digging mud flats at low tide.

mussel.name: Mussel
mussel.description: Blue-black shellfish that clings in dense colonies.
mussel.blurb: Mussels attach with golden threads called byssus — the same protein once woven into luxury fabric in ancient times.

crab.name: Crab
crab.description: Sweet claw and body meat behind a hard carapace.
crab.blurb: Maryland blue crab feasts are social rituals — newspaper on the table, mallets in hand, and patience for picking every morsel.

recipes.description: You crushed the potato into a rough, starchy mash.
recipes.tip: Smash starchy tubers to break down fibers before mixing or cooking.

mashed_potato.name: Mashed Potato
mashed_potato.description: Broken-down potato flesh — soft, dense, and ready to blend.
mashed_potato.blurb: Mashing releases starch that thickens stews and binds simple hearth dishes together.

recipes.description: The apple blistered and darkened over open heat.
recipes.tip: Char fruit over flame to deepen sweetness before finishing a dish.

charred_apple.name: Charred Apple
charred_apple.description: Smoke-kissed apple with caramelized edges and softened flesh.
charred_apple.blurb: A quick sear over coals concentrates sugars — a hearth cook's shortcut to depth.

recipes.description: The seeds swelled and split, sending out pale shoots.
recipes.tip: Soak seeds in fresh water to coax them into sprouting.

sprouted_seeds.name: Sprouted Seeds
sprouted_seeds.description: Seeds soaked in water until tiny shoots emerge.
sprouted_seeds.blurb: Sprouting wakes dormant enzymes — a gentle first step toward porridge and tonics.

recipes.description: Berries and spring water mingled into a fragrant brew.
recipes.tip: Combine ripe berries with clean spring water for a simple restorative drink.

berry_brew.name: Berry Brew
berry_brew.description: A warm infusion of crushed berries and spring water.
berry_brew.blurb: Hearth cooks steeped wild fruit in hot water long before tea leaves crossed the mountains.

recipes.description: Sprouted seeds broke down into a mellow, drinkable tonic.
recipes.tip: Blend sprouted seeds with spring water for a filling camp drink.

seed_tonic.name: Seed Tonic
seed_tonic.description: A milky, nourishing drink from sprouted seeds and water.
seed_tonic.blurb: Travelers carried soaked seed tonics when fresh bread was days away.

recipes.description: Mash and charred fruit came together into a smoky-sweet hearth dish.
recipes.tip: Fold charred fruit into mash for a finished fireside plate.

hearth_mash.name: Hearth Mash
hearth_mash.description: Charred fruit folded into creamy mashed potato.
hearth_mash.blurb: Sweet and smoke over starch — a rustic plate born at the edge of the fire.

recipes.description: Carrot and water simmered into a clear, sweet broth.
recipes.tip: Steep a root vegetable in spring water for a quick broth.

carrot_broth.name: Carrot Broth
carrot_broth.description: A golden broth steeped from carrot and spring water.
carrot_broth.blurb: Simple root broths sustained field workers before stock pots became kitchen fixtures.

recipes.description: Mash and water loosened into a simple, filling stew.
recipes.tip: Thin mashed tubers with spring water for a quick stew.

tuber_stew.name: Tuber Stew
tuber_stew.description: Hearty mash thinned with spring water into a warming stew.
tuber_stew.blurb: Stretching mash with water was the oldest trick for feeding one more mouth at the table.

achievements.name: First Cut
achievements.description: Separate a primal ingredient into its first raw piece.
achievements.hint: Drag Berries to the counter and use Separate.

achievements.name: Plated Up
achievements.hint: Combine and cook discoveries until a recipe appears in the cabinet.

achievements.name: Stir the Pot
achievements.description: Successfully combine two ingredients on the counter.
achievements.hint: Select Combine, then drag one ingredient onto another.

achievements.name: Pantry Explorer
achievements.description: Discover 10 ingredients beyond the starter pantry.
achievements.hint: Separate primals, apply techniques, and merge pairs.

achievements.name: Pantry Master

achievements.name: Recipe Collector
achievements.hint: Follow combine and heat paths to finished recipes.

achievements.name: Recipe Aficionado
achievements.hint: Unlock Transform and push deeper into each cuisine chain.

achievements.name: Cartographer's Feast
achievements.description: Discover every ingredient and recipe in the compendium.
achievements.hint: Fill the progress map — no stone unturned.

achievements.name: Heavy Hand

achievements.name: Clean Peel

achievements.name: Hand Mixer

achievements.name: Firewalker

achievements.name: Journeyman Cook

achievements.name: Master of the Hearth

achievements.hint: Deep mastery takes patience — keep practicing.

achievements.name: Combine Artisan
achievements.hint: Merge compatible ingredients again and again.

achievements.name: Hearth Chronicler

achievements.hint: Each new discovery is stamped automatically.

achievements.name: Chart the Kitchen

achievements.name: Second Thoughts
